You are optimizing a palladium-catalysed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling run in flow, which forms a new carbon-carbon bond between an aryl halide and an organoboron partner; the active catalyst is a palladium centre bound to a phosphine ligand.

Your objective is to MAXIMIZE the reaction yield — the percentage of the limiting substrate converted to the desired coupled product.

You control the following parameters (each with its physical role and allowed range):

  - res_time — residence time (range [60, 600] s): how long reagents spend in the reactor — longer allows more conversion but also more catalyst decomposition and side-reactions
  - temperature — reactor temperature (range [30, 110] deg C): raises the reaction rate but can degrade the catalyst or promote side-pathways
  - catalyst_loading — catalyst loading (range [0.498, 2.515] mol%): how much palladium catalyst is used relative to substrate — more speeds the reaction but adds cost and can favour decomposition

turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning

**Ligand choice:** L3 dominates the top of the table. It achieves 98.7% yield (the best result overall) and consistently gives 72–91% even at moderate loading (~1.1–1.3 mol%). No other ligand exceeds 85.4% (L6). So **L3** is clearly the best ligand for this substrate.

**Temperature:** Every result above ~20% yield was obtained at 110 °C; at 30 °C essentially nothing happens (0.6%). Catalyst degradation at 110 °C is evidently not limiting for L3 within these residence times. Set **temperature = 110 °C** (max).

**Catalyst loading:** The best run (98.7%) used 2.508 mol% — the near-maximum loading. Comparing L3 rows: at ~1.1–1.3 mol% and 600 s, yields plateau around 75–91%; at ~2.5 mol% and only ~190 s, yield jumps to 83.9–98.7%. Higher Pd loading clearly accelerates the coupling faster than it promotes decomposition here. Set **catalyst_loading = 2.515 mol%** (max allowed, slightly above the 2.508 of the best run).

**Residence time:** Interestingly, L3 at 600 s with lower loading gives ~75–91%, while L3 at ~190 s with high loading gives ~99%. This suggests that at high loading and 110 °C the reaction is essentially complete by ~190 s, and longer times risk catalyst decomposition/side reactions eroding yield (consistent with L6: 85.4% at 60 s vs 75% at 600 s at the same high loading — yield *decreases* with time). So I stay close to the empirically best time, ~190 s, rather than extending it.

The best observed point (L3, 189.1 s, 110 °C, 2.508 mol% → 98.7%) is nearly optimal; I nudge loading to its maximum to squeeze out the remaining conversion while keeping residence time short enough to avoid decomposition losses.

**Final: ligand=L3, res_time=190, temperature=110, catalyst_loading=2.515**
